item.title: Long-Term Trend of Noctilucent Cloud Altitude Detected: A Comparison of Positional Data with Historical Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2610.41750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A large number of photometric and photographic position data of noctilucent clouds (NLC) obtained at 54-61 deg N, 29-50 deg E in 2020-2026 is used, comprising about 20,000 individual measurements of the altitude of NLC fragments recorded by a number of cameras. Comparison with published long-base triangulation measurements starting from 1890 reveals a descending trend in NLC altitude with a 99.5% confidence level. The current descent rate is -1.2 km per century, or half of the model prediction based on the current increase of CO2 in the atmosphere. Other factors that can influence NLC altitude are considered: solar longitude (season), local solar time, lunar tides, latitude, and solar activity. Two independent methods of NLC altitude determination based on the same photometric data are considered and compared.
item.dc:creator: Oleg S. Ugolnikov, Ilya S. Yankovsky, Maxim V. Klimenko, Egor O. Ugolnikov, Andrey M. Tatarnikov, Sergey G. Zheltoukhov

item.title: Laboratory study of mineral dust optical properties extending in the far-infrared spectral range
item.description: arXiv:2610.41907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mineral dust is one of the most abundant atmospheric aerosol types and remains a major source of uncertainty in estimates of aerosol radiative forcing. This uncertainty is particularly important in the far-infrared (FIR) spectral region, where the optical properties of natural mineral dust, especially its complex refractive index (CRI), remain poorly known. Previous measurements have commonly relied on pellet- or film-based methods, which can alter particle size, shape, and vibrational modes, inducing errors in the CRI determination. In this study, we present a laboratory investigation on six natural mineral dust samples with contrasting compositions and originated from major dust source regions worldwide, including Arizona, Atacama, China, Niger, Saudi Arabia, and Tunisia. Suspended dust aerosols were generated under controlled dry conditions and characterized using extinction spectroscopy from the infrared 250 to 4000 cm^-1 (2.5 to 40 micrometers) to the Ultraviolet-Visible (UV-Vis) from 10000 to 40000 cm^-1 (0.25 to 1 micrometer) spectral range, combined with particle size distribution measurements. The real and imaginary parts of the CRI were retrieved for all six samples, revealing a significant absorption and pronounced spectral variability in the FIR. These variations should be accounted for in remote sensing and dust radiative effect studies.
item.dc:creator: Perla Alalam, Herv\'e Herbin, Denis Petitprez, Sylvie Gosselin, Valentine Bizet, Paola Formenti, Pasquale Sellitto, Claudia Di Biagio

item.title: SATFRONT: Detecting Atmospheric Fronts with Satellite Data using Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.42111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atmospheric fronts are associated with much of the high-impact weather in the mid-latitudes, yet their identification and classification remain largely manual and subjective. Existing deep learning approaches rely primarily on gridded reanalysis or forecast data, limiting their applicability to satellite observations available for time-critical applications. We introduce SATFRONT, a machine learning framework for detecting cold, warm, and occluded fronts over Europe from geostationary satellite observations, with reanalysis data as an optional additional input. The model is trained on frontal analyses from five European national meteorological services and evaluated against UK Met Office analyses for 2024. Using satellite observations alone, SATFRONT achieves a Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.428 at a 150 km tolerance, within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services (0.277-0.501) and higher than that of an operational rule-based front detector that uses satellite data (0.133). Adding ERA5 reanalysis increases the CSI to 0.591. ERA5 substantially improves the placement of individual fronts, although its effect on their annual spatial distribution varies by front type. These results demonstrate that cold, warm, and occluded fronts can be detected directly from geostationary satellite observations, providing a basis for automated frontal analyses at the high temporal frequency required for time-critical applications.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Dravilas, Miruna Stoicescu, Roope Tervo, Carlos Horn, Oriol Hinojo Comellas, Sina Montazeri, Andrea Meraner, Ana Lucic

item.title: Value of Adding AI Weather Model Ensembles to a Multi-model Probabilistic Blend
item.description: arXiv:2610.42130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many weather forecasting organizations use a multi-model blend of ensemble members from different prediction systems to obtain a more accurate forecast. Recent studies have shown that blending deterministic AI-based models alongside physics-based models improves the overall forecast skill. However, the incorporation of an ensemble AI-based model into a multi-model blend is yet to be investigated. This study explores the value of blending the ensemble version of the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS-CRPS) with the Met Office's convection permitting physics-based ensemble, MOGREPS-UK. We show that blending site temperature (and wind speed) forecasts over the United Kingdom from both ensemble physics-based and ensemble AI-based models leads to an increase in overall forecast skill spatially, across lead times and across exceedance thresholds, especially when the models have different error characteristics. By decomposing the continuous ranked probability score of the blend into component means and diversity terms, we show that a more accurate blend can be achieved by assigning more weight to more skillful models and using models with complementary errors. For example, we show that a blend of MOGREPS-UK with either AIFS-CRPS or the physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) is better than a blend of IFS and AIFS-CRPS which are not very diverse. This has implications for the importance of weather model diversity and may lend weight to different model development approaches being pursued in tandem. We also demonstrate that calibrating AIFS-CRPS forecasts yields an increase in forecast skill comparable to calibrated ensemble physics-based forecasts, and calibrating the source forecasts before blending and the blended forecast after blending improves the overall forecast accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Harris Sop Nkuiate, Gavin Evans, Christopher A. T. Ferro, Frank Kwasniok, Caroline Bain, Stefan Siegert

item.title: Machine Learning Sensor Fusion for Water Vapor Radiometry based Tropospheric Delay Calibration
item.description: arXiv:2610.41052v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The next-generation Very Large Array (ngVLA) intends to use 22 GHz water vapor radiometry (WVR) to correct for tropospheric phase fluctuations in its high-frequency bands. However, current delay-retrieval methods do not reach the required accuracy and reliability. As a remedy, we propose a machine-learning based retrieval concept and a preliminary architecture, framed as heterogeneous, multi-rate sensor fusion. Atmospheric reanalysis profiles and surface weather set the context in which per-antenna WVR spectra are used to estimate excess path by a Kalman filter whose parameters are learned from high-cadence calibrator phases. The method is being developed, with planned first validation on the 183 GHz WVR system of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).
item.dc:creator: T. K. Sridharan, Yoshiharu Asaki, Brian E. Svoboda

item.title: An Assessment of Water Vapor Radiometry Landscape in ngVLA Context
item.description: arXiv:2610.41071v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The ngVLA intends to utilize Water Vapor Radiometry (WVR) as an approach to lower calibration overheads for tropospheric phase fluctuation correction in its high frequency bands (5 \& 6; 30.5-116 GHz) to levels below those feasible with fast switched reference gain calibration. As a stepping stone to an eventual ngVLA WVR system, the JVLA/ngVLA teams pursued an effort to develop and install a set of MMIC based compact water vapor radiometers (CWVR) and carry out on-sky testing. Most recent tests found that the CWVRs installed on the VLA antennas under this effort were non-functional in tracking visibility phases. As part of the program to develop a WVR system for the ngVLA, this memo summarizes the current landscape of water vapor radiometry experience, the situation with the CWVRs, how they relate to the ngVLA WVR requirements, and the work needed to operationalize the CWVRs as useful test systems and to make broader progress. We currently lack statistically relevant WVR correction data to understand their expected performance for the ngVLA sites. We also discuss parallel additional approaches alternative and/or complementary to the CWVRs. A path involving tests to establish the functionality, stability, sensitivity, and switched power cal/data synchronism of the CWVR system in the lab and on antenna, followed by on-sky tests, and a parallel effort to assess the utility of autocorrelation outputs of the VLA K-band receivers for delay estimation is recommended. Potential paths going beyond traditional excess path estimation methods which may be necessary to meet ngVLA requirements and goals are touched upon.
item.dc:creator: T. K. Sridharan

item.title: EnsAI: An Emulator for Atmospheric Ammonia Ensembles
item.description: arXiv:2504.16024v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensemble-based methods for data assimilation and emissions inversions are a popular way to encode flow-dependency within the model error covariance. While most ensemble methods do not require the use of an adjoint model, the need to repeatedly run a geophysical model to generate the ensemble can be a significant computational burden. In this paper, we introduce EnsAI, a new AI-based ensemble generation system for surface ammonia concentrations. When trained on an ensemble for ammonia generated by the GEM-MACH air quality model, it was shown that the ensembles produced by EnsAI can accurately reproduce the meteorology-dependent features of the original ensemble, while generating the ensemble 3,300 times faster than the original GEM-MACH ensemble. While EnsAI requires an upfront cost for generating the ensemble used for training, as well as the training itself, the long term computational savings can greatly exceed these initial computational costs. When used in an emissions inversion system, EnsAI produced similar inversion results to those in which the original GEM-MACH ensemble was used while using significantly less computational resources.
item.dc:creator: Michael Sitwell

item.title: Commutative Coarse-graining on the Sphere
item.description: arXiv:2610.26896v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Filtering by spatial convolution underlies coarse-graining and Large Eddy Simulation, the analysis of multiscale dynamics, and data processing across the sciences. Yet, as commonly practiced on the sphere, it violates a basic consistency requirement: commutation with differential operators, which is necessary for deriving coarse-grained dynamics and preserving the physics across lengthscales. The root of the problem is nonlocality of filtering, which compares directions in different tangent planes. The same reason underlies the Foucault pendulum's precession, and it is why the commutation failure is intrinsically geometric rather than being due to the coordinate system or numerical grid. A recently proposed generalized spherical convolution is, for a given scalar kernel, the unique linear operator commuting with the radial projection, divergence, and curl. Any consistent linear operator, be it spectral truncation, wavelet transform, diffusion, Green's-function inversion, or a machine-learned convolution, necessarily takes this form. From a simulation of an unstable jet, we demonstrate commutation to within numerical round-off, whereas common filtering that ignores curvature produces significant spurious divergence where none exists and gradient errors comparable to the gradients themselves.
item.dc:creator: Chayut Teeraratkul, Hussein Aluie

item.title: Satellite-derived bathymetry of Arabian Gulf ports under leakage-free validation: a multi-site benchmark of empirical, machine-learning and deep-learning models against 285,000 multibeam soundings, with an outlook for UAE waters
item.description: arXiv:2610.33609v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) is often proposed as a low-cost complement to multibeam surveys of ports, but its accuracy is seldom measured on an area the model has never seen. We test SDB in the turbid, shallow and tidal waters of the Abu Dhabi coast against 285,619 multibeam soundings from twelve surveys at six port areas, reduced to Lowest Astronomical Tide. The Stumpf ratio, the Lyzenga transform, a monotonic gradient-boosted tree model (LightGBM) and a U-Net ensemble were trained on 72 Sentinel-2 images and tested in transfer to an unseen site and with local control (about 20% of a site's soundings, spatial blocks beyond a 225 m buffer). The validation design changed the result more than the model: the same LightGBM model gave 0.57 m RMSE under a random pixel split, 1.30 m under spatial blocks and 1.66 m at an unseen site. In transfer the Stumpf ratio (1.45 m) was not beaten by LightGBM, the U-Net or Lyzenga. With local control a hybrid of the tree output and the band ratio reached 1.11 m over 0-11 m, 67% of pixels within the IHO S-44 Order 2 tolerance and a conformal 95% interval with 95% observed coverage; in clear water it reached 0.29-0.53 m. The seabed could not be read beyond 11 m, and summer images were five to six times more turbid than winter ones. ICESat-2 ATL24 agreed with the surveys to 0.25 m after a depth-dependent offset was removed. A 60 m reconnaissance mosaic of 17,200 km2 of the UAE coast, calibrated cell by cell on ICESat-2 without any vessel survey, reached 1.42 m RMSE on held-out blocks over half of the product. Sentinel-2 SDB with about a hundred control depths per image is a usable reconnaissance and change-monitoring tool in these waters to about 10 m; it does not meet S-44 Order 1 without local control, and accuracies from random splits should not be taken as operational accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Saeed, Mohamed H. Alhosani, Dmitry Mikhaylov, Yasser F. Al Wahedi
